Great questions — answers below and attaching a short one-pager and the POC plan.

1) SLA summary (Redwood Dedicated):
- Throughput/latency: contractual P95/P99 latency targets per route (example: P95 < 120ms, P99 < 220ms) tied to capacity reservation tiers.
- Capacity guarantees: reserved GPU pools with autoscale headroom and burst credits; contractual minimum throughput and rapid remediation/playbook for saturation.
- Remedies: service credits for SLA misses and priority failover to adjacent capacity regions.

2) Hyperscaler reserved instances:
- Reserved VMs provide baseline capacity but do not include an inference runtime that does continuous batching/KV-cache across requests — meaning higher per-token cost in practice.
- Preemption risk only applies to spot instances; reserved/committed instances remove preemption but still face transient regional resource contention during sudden demand spikes (customers see throttling or queueing).
- Typical mitigation is client-side sharding or queueing which increases latency and complexity. We have case studies (see attached redwood_vs_hyperscaler-1pager.pdf).

3) Procurement timeline:
- Typical path: POC (2–3 weeks) -> SOW + pricing review (1 week) -> MSA signature (1–2 weeks) depending on legal review.
- We can provide a Docusign-ready MSA and a short SOW template to accelerate.

Recommended POC tests (technical):
- End-to-end lat/throughput at 50k concurrent users simulated for 30m windows.
- KV cache hit-rate test to measure effective token reduction.
- Failover test across regions.
- Cost measurement: measure tokens generated and compute $/1k tokens in each config.

I've attached the POC plan and a ballpark dedicated quote. If that looks good, let's tentatively lock Aug 10 for kickoff.

Attachments: redwood_vs_hyperscaler-1pager.pdf, acme_poc_plan.pdf, acme_dedicated_quote.xlsx

Best,
Markus
